segments.title: 같은 빠르기로 도는데 왜 가속도일까
segments.text: An object on the edge of a rotating platform can keep the same speed while continually changing direction. Its motion is redirected inward at every instant. From that scene, we will derive why centripetal acceleration points toward the center, how speed and radius change its magnitude, and how to describe rotation around a three-dimensional axis. Finally, worked problems will connect this picture to units and calculus.

segments.title: 입자의 원운동 모형
segments.text: Track one point on the rotating object, ignoring its size and spin for now. Model it as a particle on a circle. Call the radius r and its speed along the circle s. Speed is the length of the velocity vector, whose direction is tangent to the circle at every point. That tangent is perpendicular to the radius.

segments.text: Take two nearby positions. Their velocity arrows have equal lengths but different directions. Translate both arrows to a common tail, then draw the change from the earlier arrow tip to the later tip. That is delta velocity. The triangle formed by the two radii and the one formed by the velocity vectors have the same included angle, so they are similar.

segments.title: 짧은 현이 호에 가까워지는 과정
segments.text: Similarity gives the magnitude of delta velocity over speed equal to the magnitude of delta position over radius. The straight line between positions is a chord; the traveled distance is an arc. For a finite interval the chord is shorter, so they are not equal. As the interval approaches zero, chord length divided by elapsed time approaches instantaneous speed. That limit makes the acceleration result exact.

segments.title: 구심가속도의 크기와 방향
segments.text: Acceleration is the limit of velocity change divided by elapsed time. The expression becomes speed over radius times speed: speed squared over radius. The velocity difference points inward at the midpoint of the nearby positions, and in the limit it points exactly toward the center. This inward acceleration is centripetal acceleration. Constant speed still permits acceleration because velocity direction changes.

segments.text: At ten meters per second on a five-meter radius, centripetal acceleration is twenty meters per second squared. Double speed at the same radius and acceleration quadruples. Double radius at the same speed and it halves, because the turn is gentler. Centripetal acceleration does not name a new physical force. The net effect of forces such as tire friction or string tension produces the required inward acceleration.

segments.text: Circular position can also be described by an angle. At angle theta, x is r cosine theta and y is r sine theta. For constant angular velocity omega, theta equals the initial angle plus omega t. Omega is measured in radians per second, with its sign distinguishing rotation direction. Speed is nonnegative, so its relationship to omega uses the magnitude of omega.

segments.text: Differentiate the position with respect to time. Cosine becomes minus sine and sine becomes cosine, while the chain rule contributes omega from the changing angle. Differentiate again and both components contain minus r omega squared times their original cosine or sine. Acceleration is therefore minus omega squared times the radius vector: inward, with magnitude r omega squared. This matches the geometric derivation.

segments.text: One revolution covers two pi r, so its period is two pi r divided by speed. Frequency, revolutions per second, is the reciprocal. Multiply frequency by two pi radians per revolution to obtain angular-speed magnitude. Period is in seconds, frequency in hertz, and angular speed in radians per second. They describe the same motion but are different quantities.

segments.text: Cross-product direction depends on order and coordinate convention. This diagram uses a right-handed frame: x right, y up, and z out of the screen. segments.title: 왜 외적 크기가 속력과 같을까
segments.text: Cross-product magnitude is the product of vector lengths and the sine of their angle. For a circular radius perpendicular to the axis, the sine is one, leaving angular speed times radius, exactly our speed relation. A position component parallel to the axis contributes nothing to the cross product. The effective circular radius is the component perpendicular to the rotation axis.

segments.text: Conversely, given a point’s radius and velocity in genuine circular motion, divide radius crossed with velocity by radius length squared. The radius must be nonzero, and the order is now radius followed by velocity. Radius two and speed six give angular speed three. Doubling both radius and speed quadruples both numerator and denominator, leaving the same angular velocity.

segments.text: One point’s velocity cannot determine every possible angular-velocity component. Adding rotation around an axis parallel to that point’s radius does not change its velocity. Applied to arbitrary motion, the expression extracts the tangential change seen about the chosen reference point.
